name: Multispectral imager, 7 bands (MultiScape100 class)
tooltip: A 7-band camera that sees about 4.75 m detail from 500 km, enough to tell flooded land from dry and healthy crops from stressed ones. It makes data that must be sent home before it can be used.
source: mass, imaging power 5.8 W (average 3.0 W is estimate), storage: https://satcatalog.com/component/multiscape100-cis/; data 0.75 GB/day estimate from NAPA-2 (about 250 MB per image session, 3 sessions): https://nanosat11th.itu.edu.tr/assets/papers/NAPA-2.pdf; cost: estimate; science: game value

name: Hyperspectral imager (HyperScape100 class)
tooltip: Splits light into many more colours, so it can detect crop disease and water quality that a normal camera misses. It also produces far more data and uses more power.
source: mass, peak power 7.75 W (average 4.5 W is estimate): https://space.oscar.wmo.int/instruments/view/hyperscape100; data, storage, cost: estimate; science: game value

name: Body-mounted solar panels (6U)
tooltip: Solar cells fixed to the sides of the satellite. Simple and cheap, but only a small area faces the Sun at any time, so they make little power.
source: generation 19.4 W peak in LEO: https://endurosat.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Endurosat_Product_Catalogue_02_22.pdf; mass, cost: estimate

name: Deployable solar array (6U)
tooltip: Wings that unfold after launch to catch more sunlight, giving about twice the power for about twice the mass. A more complex mechanism that has to deploy correctly.
source: generation 38.4 W peak, mass 0.655 to 1.065 kg (upper value used), list price $51,300: https://satsearch.co/products/endurosat-6u-deployable-solar-array

name: Power system with 20 Wh battery
tooltip: Stores solar energy for the part of each orbit spent in Earth's shadow, about 34 minutes at this altitude. Only about 60% of the capacity is treated as usable.
source: mass 0.298 kg including power electronics, capacity 20.4 Wh (EPS I Plus): https://www.endurosat.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/EnduroSat_Products_Presentation_07_22.pdf; power draw 0.1 W (about 0.074 W per https://unisec-global.org/pdf/uniglo11/presentation/day1/10_SLINQI.pdf); cost: estimate

name: Power system with 84 Wh battery
tooltip: A battery about four times larger, for loads that must keep running through eclipse, or for brief high-power use such as an ion thruster. It is also over four times heavier.
source: mass 1.28 kg including power electronics, capacity 84 Wh (EPS II): https://www.endurosat.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/EnduroSat_Products_Presentation_07_22.pdf; cost: estimate

name: S-band transmitter, about 3.4 Mbps
tooltip: A common, low-cost radio. At 3.4 Mbps it can send roughly 1 GB per day to a single ground station, enough for a simple camera but not for a hyperspectral one.
source: data rate up to 3.4 Mbps: https://www.cubesatshop.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/Communication-systems-Brochure-v1.pdf; mass 0.15 kg, average power 2.0 W (about 8 W while transmitting), cost: estimate

name: X-band transmitter, up to 50 Mbps
tooltip: A faster radio that sends about 15 times more data per pass, as Planet's Doves do. It needs more power and a slightly larger antenna.
source: mass under 130 g plus patch antenna 53 g, data rate 10 to 50 Mbps: https://copernical.com/product-public/item/download/40_5c4939c11a3cebfe149d3d0ead0b28ee, https://cta.ing.unlp.edu.ar/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CUBESAT-6U-v5.pdf; transmit power below 10 W: https://core.ac.uk/download/32550235.pdf (average 3.5 W is estimate); cost: estimate

name: Onboard computer
tooltip: Runs the spacecraft, stores images until they can be sent, and handles commands from the ground.
source: mass 65 g, power 1 W: https://cta.ing.unlp.edu.ar/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/CUBESAT-6U-v5.pdf; storage 2 GB: https://nanosat11th.itu.edu.tr/assets/papers/NAPA-2.pdf; cost: estimate

name: Computer with FPGA data processor
tooltip: Processes images on board so only useful results are sent home. That saves downlink time but needs more power.
source: power: OBC 0.9 W plus FPGA 3 W: https://unisec-global.org/pdf/uniglo11/presentation/day1/10_SLINQI.pdf; mass, storage 32 GB, cost: estimate

name: 3-axis attitude control (CubeADCS small class)
tooltip: Wheels and sensors that point the camera at the ground. Accuracy of about 1 degree is fine for wide scenes but blurs fine detail.
source: mass 0.55 kg, pointing under 1 degree: https://nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/5.soa_gnc_2021.pdf; power 1.4 W (upper end of 0.4 to 1.4 W range for this class) and cost: estimate; pointing 0.4: game value

name: Precision attitude control (XACT-15 class)
tooltip: A star tracker and precision wheels that point about 300 times more accurately, giving sharper and better-aimed images. It costs more and weighs more.
source: mass 0.885 kg, pointing 0.003 to 0.007 degrees: https://nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/5.soa_gnc_2021.pdf; power, cost: estimate; pointing 0.98: game value

name: Cold iodine thruster (I2T5 class)
tooltip: A tiny thruster for small orbit corrections. Its total impulse is about 75 N-s, enough for roughly 7 m/s on a satellite this size, so it slows orbit decay but cannot change orbit.
source: wet mass 0.9 kg, 5 W firing (1 W standby), total impulse under 75 N-s: https://satsearch.co/products/thrustme-i2t5-cold-iodine-thruster; delta-v about 75 N-s divided by about 10.5 kg, cost: estimate

name: Iodine ion thruster (NPT30-I2 class)
tooltip: Far more efficient than a cold gas thruster and able to hold altitude for months, but it needs about 55 W while firing, more than the solar panels alone can supply, so the battery has to cover it.
source: mass 1.2 kg including propellant, 55 W nominal, 0.8 mN: https://link.springer.com/10.1038/s41586-021-04015-y; average power 10 W, delta-v 100 m/s, cost: estimate (no confirmed total impulse found)

name: Passive thermal control (MLI and radiators)
tooltip: Insulating blankets and radiators that need no power. Works if the satellite's temperature stays in a narrow range.
source: design approach: https://unisec-global.org/pdf/uniglo11/presentation/day1/10_SLINQI.pdf; mass, cost: estimate

name: Active thermal control (heaters)
tooltip: Heaters keep the battery and electronics warm through eclipse, which extends battery life but uses power.
source: heated battery pack approach: https://unisec-global.org/pdf/uniglo11/presentation/day1/10_SLINQI.pdf; mass, power, cost: estimate

name: X-band SAR, stripmap
tooltip: A radar that makes its own illumination, so it images through clouds and darkness, and it is well suited to mapping sea ice and ocean surfaces. It draws far more power than a camera and makes lots of data.
source: scaled from ICEYE class (85 to 110 kg satellite, 3.2 kW peak radiated power, 345 W peak solar, 1.4 kWh battery, 140 to 500 Mbps X-band): https://sar.iceye.com/5.0/productguide/fleet, https://iceye.us/who-we-are/technology; average power 150 W assumes about 30% duty on a 500 W peak; mass, cost, data, storage: estimate

name: X-band SAR, high resolution
tooltip: A wider-bandwidth radar that resolves finer detail and more modes. It needs about twice the power and produces about twice the data.
source: scaled from ICEYE class (85 to 110 kg satellite, 3.2 kW peak radiated power, 345 W peak solar, 1.4 kWh battery, 140 to 500 Mbps X-band): https://sar.iceye.com/5.0/productguide/fleet, https://iceye.us/who-we-are/technology; average power 270 W assumes about 30% duty on a 900 W peak; mass, cost, data, storage: estimate

name: Fixed solar array, about 345 W peak
tooltip: Fixed panels like ICEYE's. Averaged over an orbit they supply less than the radar needs while imaging, so the radar can run only part of each orbit.
source: 345 W peak: https://iceye.us/who-we-are/technology; mass, cost: estimate

name: Large solar array, about 700 W peak
tooltip: Roughly twice the area. More imaging time, but heavier and more expensive, and it pushes the satellite toward the mass limit.
source: estimate: about twice the ICEYE-class array

name: 1.4 kWh Li-ion battery
tooltip: A large battery stores energy between radar passes and carries the satellite through eclipse.
source: 1.4 kWh: https://iceye.us/who-we-are/technology; mass about 12 kg at roughly 115 Wh/kg, cost: estimate

name: 2.8 kWh Li-ion battery
tooltip: Twice the storage allows longer radar imaging per orbit, but adds about 12 kg.
source: estimate: twice the ICEYE-class battery

name: X-band downlink, 140 Mbps
tooltip: Fast enough to send tens of gigabytes per day through a single ground station.
source: 140 Mbps (ICEYE Gen2): https://sar.iceye.com/5.0/productguide/fleet; mass, cost estimate; average power 12 W assumes about 40 W while transmitting

name: X-band downlink, 500 Mbps
tooltip: More than three times the rate, needed when the radar produces more data than a 140 Mbps link can send in the available contact time.
source: 500 Mbps: https://iceye.us/who-we-are/technology; mass, cost estimate; average power 25 W assumes about 70 W while transmitting

name: Onboard computer and data recorder
tooltip: Controls the satellite and stores radar data until it can be downlinked.
source: estimate

name: Computer with onboard SAR processor
tooltip: Processes radar data on board and stores much more of it.
source: estimate

name: Reaction wheels and star tracker
tooltip: Points the radar antenna toward the target area to within a fraction of a degree.
source: estimate

name: High-agility pointing system
tooltip: Faster and more precise pointing lets the satellite image more targets per orbit, at the cost of mass and power.
source: estimate; ICEYE relies on satellite agility plus electronic beam steering: https://sar.iceye.com/5.0/productguide/fleet

name: Cold gas thruster
tooltip: Small corrections only. It cannot hold altitude for years.
source: estimate

name: Ion propulsion for orbit maintenance
tooltip: Keeps the orbit in its precise ground track over the mission. ICEYE uses ion propulsion for this. It needs power and more mass.
source: ICEYE uses ion propulsion for orbit maintenance: https://sar.iceye.com/5.0/productguide/fleet; mass, power, delta-v, cost: estimate

name: Passive thermal control and radiators
tooltip: Radiators carry away radar electronics heat with no moving parts.
source: estimate

name: Active thermal control with heat pipes
tooltip: Heat pipes and heaters hold the radar electronics at a stable temperature when the radar is switched on and off.
source: estimate

name: Narrow-angle camera pair (LROC NAC class)
tooltip: Two black-and-white cameras that see features about half a metre across from 50 km, good enough to survey landing sites. Compact, but they produce much less science than a full instrument suite.
source: 2 cameras at 8.2 kg and 6.4 W each (peak shown, average 8 W is estimate) from the data brief (LROC factsheet; not re-verified); 0.5 m per pixel from 50 km: https://www.lroc.asu.edu/assets/LROC_instrument_overview-5b07a1035bc2625c486e7f3d5777034224aa9b6ea887b61fcfd962f863c675f9.pdf; cost, data, storage: estimate

name: Full instrument suite (cameras, laser altimeter, radiometer)
tooltip: The full set of LRO-class instruments gives maps of the surface, topography and temperature. It is much heavier, uses much more power and returns a lot more data.
source: payload mass 92.6 kg: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter; total payload power about 125 W: https://webarchive.library.unt.edu/eot2008/20080916013832/http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/database/MasterCatalog?sc=LUNARRO; cost, data, storage: estimate

name: Fixed solar array, about 900 W
tooltip: Smaller fixed array. Enough for a light payload, but little spare power.
source: scaled from LRO (launch 1,916 kg, dry 1,018 kg, payload 92.6 kg, 1,850 W array, 800 W orbit average): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter, https://eoportal.org/satellite-missions/lro; generation, mass, cost: estimate (about half of LRO)

name: Articulated solar array, 10.7 m2
tooltip: A large array that follows the Sun gives much more power. LRO's array made about 1,850 W at end of life and about 800 W averaged over its orbit.
source: 10.7 m2 array, 1,850 W: https://eoportal.org/satellite-missions/lro, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter; mass, cost: estimate

name: Li-ion battery, about 2.2 kWh
tooltip: Carries the spacecraft through the long lunar eclipses.
source: capacity about 80 Ah at 28 V (one source gives 80 Ah, another 126 Ah): https://eoportal.org/satellite-missions/lro; mass, cost: estimate

name: Li-ion battery, about 3.5 kWh
tooltip: A larger battery with more reserve for the 48 minutes of eclipse per orbit.
source: 126 Ah, 35 kg: https://eoportal.org/satellite-missions/lro (voltage 28 V is an assumption); cost: estimate

name: S-band and low-rate X-band link
tooltip: Enough to send routine data, but too slow for a full instrument suite.
source: estimate

name: High-rate link, about 100 Mbps
tooltip: A high-rate link with a steerable dish can return every instrument's data, but it needs more power and a precisely pointed antenna.
source: estimate (high-rate lunar links are on the order of 100 Mbps)

name: Radiation-tolerant flight computer
tooltip: Radiation-tolerant computer; LRO flew a 133 MHz RAD750.
source: LRO flight computer: https://pds.nasa.gov/data/pds3/releases/backup/2016/201604.lrolola/insthost.cat; mass, power, storage, cost: estimate

name: Larger flight computer and recorder
tooltip: More processing and a much larger data recorder, to store data while the Moon blocks the line to Earth.
source: estimate

name: Reaction wheels and star trackers
tooltip: Points the spacecraft at the Moon and the antenna at Earth.
source: estimate

name: Precision pointing system
tooltip: Allows the finest imaging, with higher mass and power.
source: estimate

name: Hydrazine system, small tanks
tooltip: Enough for lunar orbit insertion and little else. Propellant mass is added by the rocket equation.
source: estimate; propellant mass from fuel = dry mass x (e^(delta-v / (Isp x 9.81)) - 1) with Isp about 220 s (assumption)

name: Hydrazine system, large tanks
tooltip: Enough for orbit insertion and a year of orbit maintenance. About 1,360 m/s is what LRO's launch and dry masses imply at 220 s specific impulse.
source: delta-v calculated from LRO masses 1,916 and 1,018 kg: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Reconnaissance_Orbiter; Isp 220 s assumed; mass, power, cost: estimate

name: Passive thermal control
tooltip: Blankets and radiators handle the sunlit side and the cold of lunar eclipse only in a narrow range.
source: estimate

name: Active thermal control
tooltip: Heaters and heat pipes hold the instruments at a stable temperature through eclipse.
source: estimate
